Recognizing that the situation had escalated beyond immediate containment, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), working alongside local community groups and charitable organizations, mobilized a late-night rescue operation. Police minibuses were brought in to retrieve the terrified residents from their damaged properties.

The 113 displaced individuals—which included more than 40 children—were initially taken to the City Church on University Avenue, where volunteers provided food, clothing, bedding, and medical attention. Later, due to ongoing safety concerns, authorities transferred the group to a secure, undisclosed leisure center in Northern Ireland for protection while long-term arrangements were made. Many of the victims, traumatized by the ordeal, expressed a desire to return to Romania immediately, stating they no longer felt safe in the region.

### Political Outrage and National Response

The dramatic displacement of an entire ethnic enclave sparked swift condemnation from political leaders in Belfast and London. 

British Prime Minister Gordon Brown issued a strong statement denouncing the attacks, declaring that "there is no place for racism in modern society" and promising full support to law enforcement to bring the perpetrators to justice. Factors such as economic uncertainty, lingering paramilitary influences in working-class neighborhoods, and misinformation have fuelled anti-immigrant sentiment. 

For a city striving to present itself as a modern, welcoming European destination, the image of dozens of families being sheltered in a church hall to escape physical violence represents a profound setback.

**Dozens of Romanian families flee Belfast homes after wave of racist attacks**

**By CNN Staff**
June 18, 2009

**BELFAST, Northern Ireland (CNN)** — More than 100 Romanian immigrants, including clutching mothers and crying infants, have been forced to abandon their homes in South Belfast following a relentless campaign of racially motivated intimidation and violence, authorities and community leaders said.

The group, predominantly members of the Roma community, spent Tuesday night sleeping on the floor of a local church under police protection after a series of coordinated attacks shattered the windows of their residences, leaving families terrified for their safety.

"We cannot stay here. It is too dangerous for our children," said one Romanian man, who asked not to be identified out of fear for his safety. He described young men wearing hoods throwing bricks through windows and shouting xenophobic slurs into the middle of the night. 

"We came to Northern Ireland to build a peaceable life, but we are living in a nightmare," he told CNN through a translator.

### Escorted Under Armed Guard

The violence escalated over the weekend in the University area of South Belfast, a neighborhood that has recently seen rising tensions. On Tuesday evening, police took the extraordinary step of gathering around 115 men, women, and children and escorting them in police vans to the City Church on University Avenue. 

Local residents and church volunteers rallied through the night to provide food, blankets, and toys for the displaced families, some of whom had left their homes with nothing more than the clothes on their backs and belongings packed into plastic trash bags.

Pastor Malcolm Morgan of the City Church described the scene as heartbreaking.

"These are vulnerable people—babies, pregnant women, young children—who have been terrorized out of their living rooms," Morgan said. "The warmth shown by the volunteers represents the true spirit of Belfast, not the thugs who drove these families from their homes."

The victims were later relocated to a temporary emergency shelter at the Ozone Leisure Complex, managed by the local council, while authorities attempted to figure out a long-term solution.

### Condemnation Across Political Lines

The attacks have sparked widespread outrage across Northern Ireland, a region still working to move past decades of political and sectarian conflict known as "The Troubles." Critics worry that as traditional sectarian violence wanes, xenophobia and racism are taking its place.

Northern Ireland’s First Minister Peter Robinson and Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness issued a joint statement forcefully condemning the violence, calling the attacks "a disgrace."

"There is no place for racism in Northern Ireland," McGuinness said. "The people carrying out these cowardly attacks do not represent the vast majority of the people of Belfast, and they will not be allowed to drag this community backward."

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said it was investigating the incidents as racially motivated hate crimes and indicated that elements associated with far-right groups and local youth gangs might be responsible. Several arrests have already been made, according to PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Alistair Finlay.

"This behavior is completely unacceptable," Finlay said in a press conference. "We are putting extra patrols on the ground, and we will bring those responsible before the courts."

### Protests and an Uncertain Future

On Wednesday, hundreds of anti-racism protesters gathered outside Belfast City Hall to demonstrate solidarity with the Romanian community, carrying placards reading "Racists Out, Immigrants Welcome."

Despite the public outcry and promises of protection from the government, many of the affected families say they no longer feel safe in Northern Ireland. Local officials confirmed that a significant number of the displaced Romanians have requested assistance to leave the country and return to Romania.

For a region striving to project an image of a modern, peaceful European society, the sight of refugees fleeing their homes under police escort marks a grim chapter.

"It's a terrible indictment of where we are," said Patrick Yu, director of the Northern Ireland Council for Ethnic Minorities. "If people are being chased out of their homes simply because of who they are, then we have a very long way to go."

### 'Racist elements'

The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said they were investigating a series of racially motivated incidents, including an attack on Tuesday night where a crowd gathered outside Romanian homes shouting racist slogans and throwing stones. Local reports indicated some individuals in the crowd made Nazi salutes.

Police Superintendent Darrin Jones condemned the violence, describing it as the work of a "small minority of racist elements." 

"This behavior is totally unacceptable, and we are treating these incidents as violent hate crimes," Jones said. "We have increased patrols in the area to reassure residents and bring those responsible to justice."

Northern Ireland's First Minister Peter Robinson and Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness issued a joint statement condemning the attacks, emphasizing that racism had no place in Northern Ireland. 

"We stand unreservedly with the victims of these horrific acts," the statement read. "The people who carried out these attacks do not represent the vast majority of citizens in Belfast or Northern Ireland."

### Fearing for their lives

Many of the affected families expressed a desire to leave Northern Ireland immediately, stating they no longer felt safe in the region. 

Speaking through an interpreter, several Romanian residents said they had moved to Belfast seeking work and a better life, but now just wanted to return to Bucharest. 

"We cannot go back to those houses," one Romanian man told reporters outside the leisure center. "Our windows were broken, people were throwing bottles, and my children were screaming. We just want to go home."

Social Development Minister Margaret Ritchie, who visited the families at the O-Zone center, pledged government assistance to help accommodate those affected and assist any who wished to return to Romania.

In recent years, community groups have warned about a rise in racially motivated attacks in Northern Ireland, a region historically dominated by sectarian conflict between Protestant and Catholic communities. Community leaders have voiced concern that minority groups are increasingly becoming targets for local extremist groups and disaffected youths.
